claims.text: Conventional refractory HEAs contain high-activation elements such as tungsten and tantalum.
Tungsten and tantalum produce long-lived radionuclides under neutron irradiation.
Vanadium, titanium, and zirconium are intrinsically low-activation alternatives to tungsten and tantalum.
CALPHAD and first-principles calculations can be used to design the proposed substitution of tungsten and tantalum by vanadium, titanium, and zirconium.
Refractory HEAs possess excellent high-temperature mechanical properties.
Refractory HEAs are promising for high-temperature nuclear applications.
Conventional refractory HEAs have excellent irradiation resistance.
Tungsten- and tantalum-containing refractory HEAs suffer from high neutron activation.
Fusion plasma-facing components encounter high temperature, neutron radiation, particle and heat fluxes, and direct plasma exposure.
The relevant plasma-facing temperature is at least 1000 K.
Replacing tungsten and tantalum with vanadium, titanium, and zirconium will create stable high-temperature phases that retain mechanical integrity.
The altered elemental makeup will improve resistance to irradiation-induced defects.
Removing elements that produce long-lived radionuclides and replacing them with low-activation elements will reduce neutron-induced long-term radioactivity.
The proposed substitutions will preserve or enhance high-temperature strength.
The proposed substitutions will preserve or enhance resistance to irradiation-induced defects.
The resulting alloy will have high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance comparable to conventional refractory HEAs.
The resulting alloy will have significantly lower long-term neutron activation than conventional refractory HEAs.
The resulting low-activation refractory HEA would be viable as a structural material for fusion plasma-facing components.
Excessive substitution may compromise phase stability or mechanical strength if solubility limits are exceeded.
